rationale: The BSB renders Sarai's action at Genesis 16:6 as 'treated Hagar so harshly' and the Egyptians' action at Exodus 1:11 as 'to oppress them,' but Ellicott's note on 16:6 says the Hebrew verb behind 'treated harshly' 'is translated afflicted in Exodus 1:11,' and the Cambridge Bible calls it 'the same word as that rendered "afflict" (Genesis 15:13).' The angel's words at 16:11, 'the LORD has heard your cry of affliction,' and the LORD's words at Exodus 3:7, 'I have indeed seen the affliction of My people... I have heard them crying out,' both speak of God seeing or hearing an oppressed slave's affliction; the Pulpit Commentary on 16:11 cites Exodus 3:7 (crediting Calvin). Phyllis Trible and Tikva Frymer-Kensky, as Shai Held quotes them on TheTorah.com, read the two stories as a reversal: an Egyptian slave woman afflicted by a Hebrew mistress, and later Hebrew slaves afflicted by Egypt. Trible calls Hagar 'the precursor of Israel's plight under Pharaoh.' Held himself qualifies Frymer-Kensky's line 'Hagar is Israel': 'Hagar is not in fact Israel, and that is the point.' The target range runs from Exodus 1:11 to 3:7 so that it includes the oppression, Moses' own flight (2:15), and the verse about hearing the cry. Graded contrast_reversal because what is proposed is an inversion of roles. Graded plausible, not strong, for three reasons: Exodus never names Hagar, the BSB uses different English verbs in the two places, and the Trible and Frymer-Kensky readings were read only as Held quotes them.
